same-dataset.t: One dataset for both methods: **34 customers** (purchases per month, average spend) from overlapping groups. We will give it to K-Means and to a GMM and compare.

kmeans-centroids.t: K-Means with **K = 3** gives each customer **exactly one cluster** and summarizes each cluster by a centroid (the cross).

hard-boundaries.t: Every location belongs to its **nearest centroid**. The tinted regions have sharp edges: crossing one **flips the label**, even for nearly identical customers.

ambiguous-point.t: This customer sits where two groups overlap, but K-Means must still give it **one label**. The fact that it is borderline is not recorded.

gmm-components.t: A GMM describes the same data with **ellipses** (1 and 2 standard deviations). Each component has a **mean, a spread and a weight**.

soft-responsibility.t: The same customer gets **responsibilities for all three components** instead of one label: about **0.43 and 0.57** for the two overlapping ones.

shape-flexibility.t: The dashed circles are what K-Means implicitly assumes around its centroids. The GMM ellipses can be **wide, narrow or differently sized**, so they follow the groups more closely.

side-by-side.t: Left: K-Means, **one hard color** per customer. Right: GMM, colors **blended by responsibility**, so overlap shows as mixed colors. Both find the three groups.

when-kmeans.t: Use K-Means for **compact, similar-looking groups** when speed and simplicity matter and **one label per point** is acceptable.

when-gmm.t: Use a GMM when **overlap matters**, when you want **soft membership**, or when groups differ in spread or orientation. It has more parameters and can also stop at a local optimum.

final-summary.t: **K-Means:** hard membership, centroids, distance. **GMM:** soft membership, mean + spread + weight, responsibilities. Neither is always better, and **both need the number of groups chosen**.
